newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tobacco growers ready to hit back in election.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tobacco growers ready to hit back in election.

text.p: Caleb Chavis harvested his tobacco crop weeks ago and, in a country where smoking is under siege, is now ready to strike a blow for his livelihood in next week's U.S. presidential election.
As far as Chavis is concerned, President Bill Clinton has declared war on him. Like many other U.S. rural tobacco farmers, his vote will go to Republican challenger Bob Dole.
"Tobacco's the most important crop round here. If they take it away, a lotta people gonna hurt," says the 51-year-old farmer, standing outside his barn in the warm autumn sunshine.
"I was born a Democrat but I'm voting Republican."
Levon Pegram is a 25-year-old farm worker in North Carolina, the biggest tobacco-growing state in the country.
"I smoked for nine years and I quit. But tobacco helped pay my bills, it taught me the value of hard work and money," he says in a slow, Southern drawl.

Thousands of farmers here and in other tobacco areas like Virginia and Kentucky fear that government health measures and an increasing number of lawsuits against tobacco companies may eventually lead to the prohibition of tobacco.
With more than 400,000 people in the United States dying of smoking-related diseases every year and one in four adults indulging in the habit, many states have passed tough anti- smoking legislation.
There is no smoking on aeroplane flights within the United States, nor in most office buildings. Workers craving a fix can often be seen huddling outside on the pavement in all kinds of weather.
Cigar smoking, however, is currently seen as highly fashionable -- with film star aficionados and magazines devoted to the habit.
For Chavis and other farmers, the last straw was Clinton's decision in August to declare nicotine an addictive drug, opening the door to tighter regulation of the cigarette industry.
North Carolina, which brought in cash receipts of more than $1 billion last year from tobacco, has said it is planning to sue the federal government as a result.
Prices for tobacco this year in the state were good, giving a far better return than other crops that most small farmers also grow, like corn and beans.

Nearly one in 10 of the workforce in North Carolina, a largely agricultural state, depend on tobacco to make a living -- either by growing or transporting it, or working in the cigarette-making plants of major companies.
Some of those companies have also donated millions of dollars to the Republican Party, long considered more friendly to the tobacco industry than the Democrats.
Chavis tugs at his green baseball cap and thinks for a moment when asked about the dangers of tobacco.
"A man can drink alcohol and kill a whole family but they don't say nothing about that," he says.
"That dope business is bad, too...You've got to die of cancer or something else. I know people been smoking or chewing tobacco all their lives, it ain't done them no harm."
